paper_summary: Journal of Advanced Zoology 44(S-3), 2023, pp. 1654-1661 (page footers read 1259-1267): a Taguchi L9 / ANOVA study of the ultimate tensile strength (ASTM C297, 120 x 34 x 17 mm specimens) of Kevlar/jute/foam hybrid SANDWICH composites, varying skin material (jute+jute, jute+Kevlar, Kevlar+Kevlar), a 'density' factor (40/60/80) and reinforcement percentage (25/50/75%). Ultimate tensile strength ranged from 44 to 61 MPa, was highest for Kevlar+Kevlar skins, and ANOVA found skin material (F=10.30, p=0.088) and density (F=6.29, p=0.137) more influential than reinforcement percentage (F=3.13, p=0.242). Despite the title's use of 'syntactic foam', the core the authors actually fabricated is described in the materials section as 'Synthetic foam core material (e.g., polyurethane foam)' - a conventional blown foam - and no hollow filler particles are used anywhere in the experimental work.
extraction_notes: Marked off-topic (is_syntactic_foam_paper=false, no records) under rule 6, for the following reasons. (1) No hollow-particle filler is used by the authors. Sec. 2.1 states 'Synthetic foam core material (e.g., polyurethane foam) of specified density variations were used as main material', i.e. a conventional polymer foam core, not a hollow-particle-filled composite. Microballoons, microspheres, cenospheres and 'hollow-particle filled' appear ONLY in the introduction's literature review and in the reference list (refs 3, 18, 19, 21) - never in the authors' own materials, fabrication or results. (2) The paper conflates 'syntactic' and 'synthetic' throughout (title says 'Syntactic Foam', abstract and keywords say 'synthetic foam'), and the materials list even calls the core 'syntactic foam (Synthetic fiber) of density 1.096 g/cm3', which is internally incoherent. There is no particle grade, particle size, wall thickness, particle density or particle volume/weight fraction anywhere. (3) The work is a sandwich-panel study (Kevlar and/or jute face sheets bonded with LY556 epoxy adhesive to a foam core), i.e. a generic composite/sandwich paper rather than a hollow-particle composite paper. (4) The reported factor values are not physically interpretable as material densities: the 'Density (gm/cm3)' column of Tables 1 and 2 takes values 40, 60 and 80 g/cc, and the text repeats '40 g/cc, 60 g/cc, 80 g/cc' for the SKIN materials, which is impossible for jute or Kevlar (the same section separately gives Kevlar 1.450 g/cm3, jute 1.500 g/cm3, foam 1.096 g/cm3, resin 1.150 g/cm3). The units are evidently wrong or the factor is something other than density, so these values could not be mapped to the schema even if the paper were in scope. For reference, the tensile data that WOULD have been extractable is Table 2: jute+jute 44 / 51 / 52 MPa, jute+Kevlar 50.5 / 54 / 55 MPa, Kevlar+Kevlar 56 / 52.5 / 61 MPa at the nine Taguchi conditions; only ultimate tensile strength is reported (no modulus values are given despite being mentioned in the abstract, and Figures 5 and 6 - main effect plots for means and SN ratios - are images).
